    How to check how many inches of snow?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    To measure inches of snow, place a flat surface (snowboard or picnic table) in an open area, push a ruler vertically into the snow until it hits the surface, read the measurement to the nearest tenth of an inch, and average several spots for accuracy. You measure new snowfall during the storm and total snow depth (new + old) separately, always avoiding areas near buildings or under trees where drifts form.
     
    This video demonstrates the process of measuring snowfall:
    49s
    Iowa's News Now
    YouTube · Dec 7, 2025
    Steps for measuring new snowfall
    1. Find a spot: Choose an open, flat area away from trees, buildings, or other obstructions. 
    2. Set up: Place a flat, light-colored surface (like a snowboard or clean board) on the ground. 
    3. Measure: Push a ruler straight down into the snow until it hits the surface.
    4. Record: Note the measurement to the nearest tenth of an inch (e.g., 1.3 inches). 
    5. Repeat & average: Take several measurements in the area and average them for the most accurate reading. 
    6. Clear & repeat: Clear the surface for the next measurement, as winds and sun can alter snow density. 
    Watch this video for tips on how to accurately measure snowfall:
    1m
    WKBN27
    YouTube · Jan 16, 2025
    Key distinctions
    • Snowfall: New snow that falls during the event, measured to the nearest tenth of an inch.
    • Snow Depth: The total accumulation (new + old snow) on the ground, reported to the nearest inch, usually once a day. 
    • Water Equivalent: The amount of liquid water if the snow were melted; measured in hundredths of an inch using a special gauge.

      Who got 47 inches of snow?
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      Obihiro, Japan, in the northern island of Hokkaido, received a record-breaking 47 inches (about 120 cm) of snow in just 12 hours around February 4-5, 2025, due to a powerful cold front and sea-effect snow, causing widespread travel disruptions and significant accumulation.
       
      Key Details:
      • Location: Obihiro, Hokkaido, Japan. 
      • Timing: Early February 2025 (specifically, by the morning of February 4, 2025). 
      • Amount: 47 inches (120 cm) in 12 hours. 
      • Cause: A strong cold front combined with ocean-effect snow (similar to lake-effect snow, but over the sea). 
      • Impact: This was the highest 12-hour snowfall total ever recorded in Japan, leading to flight cancellations and travel chaos. 
      • See it: Record snowfall buries parts of Japan
        Feb 5, 2025
        FOX Weather
      • Talk about a lot of snow. ❄️❄️❄️In just 12 hours, the city of Obihiro, Japan got 47 inches (about 4 feet) of snow, the highest on record for the city, according to Japan’s Meteorological Agency. 12 hrs!!! That snow level was recorded by 9 a.m. local time on Tuesday, and the snow has not stopped since then. By 9 p.m., nearly another 2 inches of snow was recorded. This was caused by ocean effect snow. Like lake effect but cold air spills over ocean water and moves over colder land. #snOMG
